title: Death and the Dies irae
subtitle: A funeral chant: bells, bones, piano

hero.file: File:The Triumph of Death by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.jpg
hero.caption: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Triumph of Death, about 1562. Skeletons overrun a barren landscape.

intro: A single voice leads into funeral bells, rattling bows and loud piano chords. The Dies irae appears in works by Berlioz, Liszt, Saint-Saëns and Rachmaninoff, and Verdi set its Latin words in his Requiem.

stations.title: A hymn for one voice

art.file: File:The Triumph of Death by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.jpg
art.caption: Bruegel’s The Triumph of Death, about 1562. Death rides a chestnut horse ahead of an army of skeletons.

stations.text:
Gareth Hughes sings Pange lingua unaccompanied, with a breath between each Latin phrase. The stanza melody of the Eucharistic hymn returns with new words for each verse.

At Catholic funerals the Dies irae was sung to a sterner melody. Its first eight notes in the Vatican Graduale are F–E–F–D–E–C–D–D. Berlioz later set that melody low in his orchestra. In Bruegel’s The Triumph of Death, skeletons have already crossed the landscape, driving the living before them.

cues.text: Gareth Hughes sings Pange lingua, the Latin Eucharistic hymn, in a single unaccompanied line.
The stanza melody returns with new Latin words.
The melody continues through the closing stanzas to the hymn’s final prayer.

stations.title: Funeral bells in the witches’ sabbath
stations.text:
Bells toll C and G in the finale of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, in which the artist dreams of his own funeral, surrounded by witches and monsters. The Dies irae enters in the low register of the orchestra, its first statement given to four bassoons and two ophicleides, the keyed brass instruments in Berlioz’s score.

The chant is first played in long notes. The same tune is then repeated in quicker note values and passes to higher woodwind and brass. In his 1845 programme Berlioz called this a ‘burlesque parody’ of the funeral music.

cues.text: Deep bells toll C and G around the approaching funeral chant.
The Dies irae sounds low and broad, scored for four bassoons and two ophicleides.
The chant’s long notes shorten as the melody passes through the wind and brass.

stations.title: The witches’ dance
stations.text:
The witches’ round begins low in the strings, with cellos and double basses entering together. Violas answer, then violins, each group starting while the earlier players continue. The tune’s quick rise and accented turn return in different parts of the orchestra.

Later in the movement Berlioz brings the Dies irae in over this dance. In this passage the round stays in the foreground and grows louder as winds and brass join the strings. Towards the end of the passage the activity dies down into held notes, followed by quiet horn calls.

cues.text: The string parts overlap, each new entry beginning before the earlier one has finished.
Woodwinds, brass and percussion join the imitative writing in the strings.
The fast dance thins out into held notes, and then the horns bring back the chant.

stations.title: Liszt’s changing piano style
stations.text:
Liszt’s B-minor Sonata begins with low Gs and a falling scale. The piano then leaps into octaves and plays a repeated note. A few minutes later come broad D-major chords marked Grandioso.

Liszt had heard the première of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique in 1830 and transcribed it for piano in 1833. In Totentanz he wrote variations for piano and orchestra on the Dies irae. In the Sonata, beneath the broad Grandioso melody, the accompaniment continues to strike repeated quavers.

cues.text: Low Gs and falling scales begin Liszt’s B-minor Sonata, with silence between the phrases.
The piano plays leaping octaves, then strikes a repeated note.
Broad D-major chords open the Grandioso; repeated quavers continue beneath the melody.

stations.title: Death’s fiddle and rattling bows
stations.text:
Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique returns for its final rush. The wind and brass play the funeral chant in long notes while the strings race through the witches’ round. Later, violins and violas turn their bows over and strike the strings with the wood (col legno), which produces a dry rattle.

In Saint-Saëns’s Danse macabre of 1874, Death plays a solo violin and the xylophone imitates rattling bones. The woodwinds quote the Dies irae during the dance. The score grew out of a song setting of a poem by Henri Cazalis. Berlioz’s sabbath ends with the strings bowing again and the full orchestra hammering out C major.

cues.text: After the quiet horn calls, Berlioz’s orchestra builds towards the chant and round together.
Wind and brass play the funeral chant in long notes while the strings play the witches’ dance in fast figures.
Violins and violas strike their strings with the wood of their bows (col legno), which produces a dry rattle.

stations.title: Verdi: the chorus and judgement
stations.text:
Verdi’s Dies irae opens with four orchestral blows, and rushing figures lead to the entry of the chorus. The ancient Latin words describe the day of judgement, and Verdi set them to a new tune. The Requiem was first performed in the church of San Marco in Milan on 22 May 1874.

After the opening, the voices drop to a quiet dynamic at ‘Quantus tremor’ (‘how great the trembling’), where the choir repeats syllables. The orchestra keeps moving underneath.

cues.text: Verdi’s setting of the Latin judgement scene opens with four orchestral blows and rushing figures.
The orchestra plays more quietly, and the chorus’s words are heard clearly over the accompaniment.
‘Quantus tremor’ — ‘how great the trembling’ — breaks into quiet, repeated syllables.

stations.title: Three notes and a painted boat

art.file: File:Arnold Böcklin - Die Toteninsel I (Basel, Kunstmuseum).jpg
art.caption: Arnold Böcklin, Isle of the Dead, first version, 1880. A figure in a white cloak stands beside a shrouded coffin in the boat.

stations.text:
Rachmaninoff plays his C♯-minor Prelude in this 1919 recording. It opens with three low notes, A–G♯–C♯, and the answering chords are played very quietly. The right hand then plays running triplets, with a descending melody carried inside them.

Böcklin’s Isle of the Dead shows a white-cloaked figure and a coffin in a boat approaching the island. Rachmaninoff saw a black-and-white reproduction of it in 1907. His orchestral Isle of the Dead uses the Dies irae in fragments and in longer phrases. In the Prelude, the triplets lead to a return of the three opening bass notes.

cues.text: Rachmaninoff’s C♯-minor Prelude opens with A–G♯–C♯ in low octaves, followed by quiet chords.
A descending melody sounds inside the right hand’s running triplets.
The Prelude’s triplets lead to the return of its opening chords.

stations.title: Piano filling the room
stations.text:
At the return in the C♯-minor Prelude, the quiet opening chords are spread across four staves, two for each hand, and marked fff pesante, very loud and heavy. The three-note opening figure is now played in these chords.

In the Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini of 1934, Rachmaninoff gave the piano another melody of this weight. Variation VII sets the Dies irae in chords against Paganini’s tune in bassoons and plucked cellos. After its climax the Prelude grows quieter. A low C♯ is held beneath changing chords, and the final C♯-minor chord fades to ppp.

cues.text: Running triplets lead to the Prelude’s huge return, written on four staves.
A low C♯ sounds in the bass of the coda, with quieter chords above it.
